title: Cross-Session Identity Resolution in Agent Memory
summary: Cross-session identity resolution unifies persistent user identity for LLM agents, isolates users, and merges duplicate memory graphs. With runnable Mem0 code.
body_text: Say your friend likes a dark development environment and has it set on their laptop. One day you urgently log into your own mail on their laptop, and because your eyesight is weak, you switch to a light background. Ideally the system keeps both settings separately, keyed to each mail id. But if the assistant scopes memory to the laptop instead of the person , both preferences pile into one bucket and the last change wins. Your light quietly overwrites your friend's dark. When your friend logs back in, they get a light screen they never chose. That's not a storage bug, it's an identity bug across sessions. This is where Mem0 helps. Each person's facts and preferences are saved under their own user_id , so your light lives under your id and your friend's dark under theirs, no collision. Once your friend logs in with their id, the assistant is looking under the right identity and serves their dark background, not yours. Memory scopes to an id, not to a person Every memory layer partitions memory by an identifier. Mem0, for instance, scopes across four keys: user_id for the persistent account, agent_id for the agent's persona, app_id for the product surface, and run_id for a single session or ticket. You write under an id, you read back under the same id. mem . add ( "I prefer dark mode and terse code reviews." , user_id = "user_abc" ) mem . search ( "how does this user like reviews?" , user_id = "user_abc" ) mem . add ( "I prefer dark mode and terse code reviews." , user_id = "user_abc" ) mem . search ( "how does this user like reviews?" , user_id = "user_abc" ) mem . add ( "I prefer dark mode and terse code reviews." , user_id = "user_abc" ) mem . search ( "how does this user like reviews?" , user_id = "user_abc" ) This works perfectly, and that's exactly what hides the problem. The store hands back whatever lives under the id you gave it. It has no opinion about whether user_abc is the right id for the human actually typing right now. Passing a user_id isn't the same as knowing who the user is. One is a lookup key. The other is a decision, and the store doesn't make it for you. Mem0's identifiers scope memory, they don't resolve or merge identities across sessions, and honestly that's the right split: you don't want your memory store guessing who you are. That guessing is a layer you own. So persistent user identity for an agent isn't a field you set once. It's a mapping you keep maintaining, from every messy signal a real person shows up with to the one canonical identity their memory should hang on. Two people, one computer Here's the failure in its most concrete form. One shared machine, two people. —> Checkout complete code on GitHub <— Monday, Person A signs in and tells the assistant they write Python and want a dark editor background. Thursday, Person B signs in on the same machine and says dark hurts their eyes, they want light. Saturday, Person A comes back. What background do they get? The whole answer hangs on one decision you made when you wrote that memory: which id you scoped it to. Scope it to the machine and both people write into the same bucket. A's dark and B's light end up in one place, and B's was the last write in. A comes back to a light editor they never asked for. That's not a preferences glitch. It's one person's setting bleeding into another's, on the exact store that was supposed to make the thing feel personal. Scope it to the person and A's preference lives under A's id, B's under B's, and the two never touch. # wrong: one bucket for the shared machine mem . add ( "I prefer a dark editor background." , user_id = "shared-pc" ) # Person A mem . add ( "I prefer a light editor background." , user_id = "shared-pc" ) # Person B, overwrites # right: one bucket per person mem . add ( "I prefer a dark editor background." , user_id = "user_abc" ) # Person A mem . add ( "I prefer a light editor background." , user_id = "user_def" ) # Person B # wrong: one bucket for the shared machine mem . add ( "I prefer a dark editor background." , user_id = "shared-pc" ) # Person A mem . add ( "I prefer a light editor background." , user_id = "shared-pc" ) # Person B, overwrites # right: one bucket per person mem . add ( "I prefer a dark editor background." , user_id = "user_abc" ) # Person A mem . add ( "I prefer a light editor background." , user_id = "user_def" ) # Person B # wrong: one bucket for the shared machine mem . add ( "I prefer a dark editor background." , user_id = "shared-pc" ) # Person A mem . add ( "I prefer a light editor background." , user_id = "shared-pc" ) # Person B, overwrites # right: one bucket per person mem . add ( "I prefer a dark editor background." , user_id = "user_abc" ) # Person A mem . add ( "I prefer a light editor background." , user_id = "user_def" ) # Person B When A comes back, the only thing deciding dark or light is the id you search under: mem . search ( "editor background?" , filters = { "user_id" : "shared-pc" } ) # -> light, B's, contaminated mem . search ( "editor background?" , filters = { "user_id" : "user_abc" } ) # -> dark, A's own mem . search ( "editor background?" , filters = { "user_id" : "shared-pc" } ) # -> light, B's, contaminated mem . search ( "editor background?" , filters = { "user_id" : "user_abc" } ) # -> dark, A's own mem . search ( "editor background?" , filters = { "user_id" : "shared-pc" } ) # -> light, B's, contaminated mem . search ( "editor background?" , filters = { "user_id" : "user_abc" } ) # -> dark, A's own Same store, same two facts. That one scope key is the whole difference between a personal agent and a leaky one. Scoping to the user, which is exactly what Mem0's user_id gives you, is what keeps A on dark and B on light. This is identity resolution doing its most basic job: settling "who is this" before it ever gets to "what do they like." Wanna give it a try? Get a Mem0 API Key and try it yourself. What identity resolution actually has to do Fellegi and Sunter framed identity resolution back in 1969 as a decision with three outcomes for every candidate pair, link, don't link, or send to review, chosen to keep the error rates on both sides in check. In practice it splits into deterministic matching (the emails are identical, link them) and probabilistic matching (same device, same name, close enough, score it). You've almost certainly used the productized version without calling it that. Every customer-data platform, Segment, Mixpanel, all of them, runs an identity graph that stitches an anonymous device to a known account the second there's enough signal. Same deterministic-then-probabilistic machinery. Agent memory just inherited the problem one level down, at the user, and it shows up as three jobs. Unify: The same human keeps arriving under different signals: a guest token, then an email, then an SSO subject, then a second device. They all need to resolve to one identity, or the memory scatters into fragments that each look like a brand-new user. Isolate: Two different humans must never land on the same identity. A shared family tablet, a generic support@ inbox, one too-eager merge, and suddenly one person's memory is scoped to someone else's id. In a memory system that isn't a glitch, it's a leak. Merge: When you find out two ids were the same person all along, maybe a guest who just signed in, maybe a duplicate account nobody caught, you have to fold one memory graph into the other and retire the empty one, without dropping anything and without counting it twice. Get these right and memory feels personal the way people actually want. Get unify wrong and the agent has amnesia. Get isolate wrong and you've got a confidentiality breach. Fuzzy match If every returning user politely logged in with the same email every time, this would be a lookup, not a problem. What is they don't.? What if they browse anonymously and buy later? or They start on web and finish on mobile? or They sign up once with a work email and again through SSO? Most of the signal you get is partial, and every interesting decision lives in the gap between "obviously the same person" and "obviously not." That gap is where you need scoring. Weight each signal, add up what an incoming session shares with a known identity, and check the total against two thresholds: Above the link threshold: confident enough to unify on the spot. Below the no-link threshold: treat as a new person. In between: review . Don't auto-merge. That middle band isn't a failure, it's your safety valve. A verified email is deterministic and should link on its own. A shared device is much weaker, because a shared device is exactly how two people get confused for each other, so it should drop a candidate into review, not link it. Name plus device together can clear the bar; device alone shouldn't. Concretely: W_EMAIL , W_DEVICE , W_NAME = 1.0 , 0.5 , 0.3 LINK , REVIEW = 0.8 , 0.4 def resolve ( signals , profile ) : if signals . get ( "email" ) in profile [ "emails" ] : return "link" # deterministic, score 1.0 score = 0.0 if signals . get ( "device" ) in profile [ "devices" ] : score += W_DEVICE if signals . get ( "name" ) == profile [ "name" ] : score += W_NAME if score >= LINK : return "link" # e.g. device + name if score >= REVIEW : return "review" # e.g. device alone: hold, don't merge return "new" W_EMAIL , W_DEVICE , W_NAME = 1.0 , 0.5 , 0.3 LINK , REVIEW = 0.8 , 0.4 def resolve ( signals , profile ) : if signals . get ( "email" ) in profile [ "emails" ] : return "link" # deterministic, score 1.0 score = 0.0 if signals . get ( "device" ) in profile [ "devices" ] : score += W_DEVICE if signals . get ( "name" ) == profile [ "name" ] : score += W_NAME if score >= LINK : return "link" # e.g. device + name if score >= REVIEW : return "review" # e.g. device alone: hold, don't merge return "new" W_EMAIL , W_DEVICE , W_NAME = 1.0 , 0.5 , 0.3 LINK , REVIEW = 0.8 , 0.4 def resolve ( signals , profile ) : if signals . get ( "email" ) in profile [ "emails" ] : return "link" # deterministic, score 1.0 score = 0.0 if signals . get ( "device" ) in profile [ "devices" ] : score += W_DEVICE if signals . get ( "name" ) == profile [ "name" ] : score += W_NAME if score >= LINK : return "link" # e.g. device + name if score >= REVIEW : return "review" # e.g. device alone: hold, don't merge return "new" That's Fellegi-Sunter in fifteen lines, and it's the whole difference between recognizing an anonymous returning user and either ignoring them or handing them someone else's memory. Tune the weights and thresholds however you like. The shape is the point: deterministic signals link outright, fuzzy signals climb toward a threshold, and there's a review band sitting in the middle for everything ambiguous. The two failure modes have very different blast radii The review band earns its place because the two ways to be wrong don't cost the same. Fragmentation is the loud, annoying one. The returning user gets treated as new, re-states everything, and walks away sure your memory feature doesn't work. You lose the retention story that justified building memory in the first place. Bad, but quiet. Collision is the scary one. When identity resolution collapses two people onto one id, one user's private context surfaces inside another user's session. Preferences are the harmless end of that. The harmful end is the health detail, the salary number, the relationship an agent inferred from one person's messages and then served to someone else, because both were typing into the same under-specified identity. That's the leak that turns a wrong merge into a security incident instead of a papercut. So the thresholds aren't arbitrary. A false merge costs far more than a missed one, so you set the link bar high, let the review band catch the ambiguous cases, and eat the occasional missed unification as the cheap mistake. An aggressive resolver chasing a slick returning-user demo optimizes the cheap failure and walks straight into the expensive one. The test: deterministic, fuzzy, review, isolate, merge So I wrote a small demo that drops this resolver in front of Mem0 and checks every job against real stored memory, not assertions. Five moves: Deterministic unify: Person A signs in on web with a verified email, stores a preference, then comes back on mobile and logs in with that same email. Deterministic match, so they link to their canonical id and the preference is just there. Fuzzy unify: Same human, but this time an anonymous web session with no email at all, only the shared web device and a name off a form. Device plus name clears the link threshold, so the resolver recognizes them without a login. I check recall two ways: naive, treating the raw session as its own id (empty), and resolved, after the fuzzy link (the preference comes back). That gap is the entire payoff of fuzzy resolution. Review, withheld: A session turns up with nothing but the shared web device. That lands in the review band, and the resolver refuses to auto-merge, because that device could just as easily be a second person on the same machine. This is the exact case an aggressive resolver leaks on. Isolate: A second human, Person B, resolves to their own id with the opposite preference. I check that Person B's id never returns Person A's memory, and I assert the leakage count is zero instead of eyeballing it. Merge duplicate graphs: Person A turns out to have two accounts, a web signup and a separate SSO signup under a different email, each with its own memory graph. A dedup pass scores the SSO account against the existing one, matches on shared device and name, and folds the two graphs into one. I check the count before and after and confirm nothing got stranded under the retired id. The only thing changing between the amnesiac agent and the one that knows its user is that resolver in the middle. Same store, same data, same model. Results Run on gpt-4o-mini with a local embedder or via API, here's what the resolver actually did: Check Result Fuzzy recall, naive (raw session id) 0 memories Fuzzy recall, resolved (fuzzy link, device + name, score 0.8) 1 memory, the preference recovered Shared-device-only session (score 0.5) held for review, not linked Cross-user leakage hits 0 Duplicate-graph merge 1 memory moved, canonical went 1 to 2, 0 stranded The row that matters is the fuzzy pair. Same human, same stored preference, and the only variable is whether an anonymous session with no email got resolved before the search ran. Naive came back empty. Resolved returned the preference. That empty cell is every returning user your agent is quietly failing to recognize just because they didn't log in first, and the resolver closed it on a device-plus-name match with no login at all. The rest is the safety side holding up. The device-only session scored 0.5 and stayed in review instead of auto-linking, which is the case that leaks. Person B resolved to their own id and saw only their own preference, none of Person A's. And when the duplicate SSO account got merged, its pricing memory moved into the canonical identity with nothing left behind, so a later search for that person returns both memories. Doing the fuzzy match responsibly Probabilistic matching is the job, but it's also where you can quietly hurt a real user. Three rules keep it honest. Let deterministic signals link, and make the fuzzy ones earn it. A verified email or an authenticated SSO subject can link on its own. A device, an IP, a name, a fingerprint, none of those should ever link alone; they accumulate toward a threshold and send the ambiguous ones to review. Tuning isn't optional here. A wrong link is a data leak, so put the bar where false merges are rare and let the review band soak up the rest. Treat a merge like a write to your most valuable record. Mem0 has no move operation, so a merge reads the memories under the source id, re-adds them under the target, and clears the source: def merge ( from_id , into_id ) : for m in mem . get_all ( user_id = from_id ) [ "results" ] : mem . add ( m [ "memory" ] , user_id = into_id ) mem . delete_all ( user_id = from_id ) def merge ( from_id , into_id ) : for m in mem . get_all ( user_id = from_id ) [ "results" ] : mem . add ( m [ "memory" ] , user_id = into_id ) mem . delete_all ( user_id = from_id ) def merge ( from_id , into_id ) : for m in mem . get_all ( user_id = from_id ) [ "results" ] : mem . add ( m [ "memory" ] , user_id = into_id ) mem . delete_all ( user_id = from_id ) Keep provenance on what you moved and which signals justified it, so a bad merge can be traced and undone instead of quietly poisoning a real account. A merge touches the record with a person's name on it. Handle it like that. Keep anonymous memory provisional. Before a session resolves to anyone, scope its memory to a session id ( run_id ) and treat it as tentative. Promote it into a real identity only once a match clears the link threshold. If it never does, it expires with the session instead of contaminating someone's account. Further reading Binette and Steorts, (Almost) All of Entity Resolution , on the deterministic-vs-probabilistic matching problem this all descends from. Fellegi and Sunter, " A Theory for Record Linkage, " JASA 64(328), 1969, the original decision-theoretic model. Rasmussen et al., Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory , on graph-based memory that dedups entity nodes inside the store. New America OTI, AI Agents and Memory , on the privacy stakes when memory crosses sessions and services. Mem0 is an intelligent, open-source memory layer designed for LLMs and AI agents to provide long-term, personalized, and context-aware interactions across sessions. Get your free API Key here: app.mem0.ai If you are an agent, sign up using mem0 init --agent --json , or self-host Mem0 from our open-source GitHub repository . Frequently asked questions Q. Isn't this what user_id is for? user_id is the destination, not the map. It tells the store where to read and write. It doesn't tell you that the anonymous mobile session is the person who was on web, or that the SSO signup is a duplicate of an account you already have. Working out which user_id a given human maps to, across signals and sessions, is the part the store leaves to you. Q. Can I match an anonymous session to a logged-in user without a login? Yes, and that's the whole point of fuzzy resolution. Score the anonymous session's signals (device, name, behavioral fingerprint) against your known identities. Clears the link threshold, unify it; lands in review, hold it; too weak, keep it separate. You get the returning user back without forcing a login, which is exactly the retention you were leaving on the table. Q. Why not just merge aggressively so returning users always get recognized? Because the two failure modes aren't symmetric. Failing to unify costs a good experience. Wrongly merging two people costs a data leak. An aggressive resolver optimizes the cheap failure and walks into the expensive one. Set the link bar high, send the ambiguous cases to review, and take the occasional missed unification as the safe error. Q. Two accounts turned out to be the same person. How do I merge their memory? Confirm the match on a strong signal first (ideally a verified email, or a review-band case a human approved), then fold one graph into the other: read every memory under the duplicate id, re-add it under the canonical one, retire the duplicate. Keep provenance so the merge stays auditable and reversible. Step five of the demo does exactly this. Q. How is identity resolution different from just isolating tenants? Tenant isolation (app or org scoping) keeps companies apart. Identity resolution works inside a tenant, keeping individual people correctly unified and separated. You need both. Nailing tenant isolation does nothing to stop two users inside the same app from colliding on an under-specified id. Q. Does the memory framework matter for this? Not much. Mem0, a graph store, your own vectors, whatever you use, the store scopes by an id and you own the mapping to it. The resolution layer sits above the store and ports across all of them.

title: Hillman to Acquire Kanebridge, Establishes Industrial Master Distribution Presence in U.S.
summary: The Hillman Group, a leading provider of hardware products and merchandising solutions, has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Kanebridge Corporation, a leading master distributor of industrial fasteners for a purchase price of $315 million, subject to customary adjustments for cash, indebtedness, working capital and transaction expenses.
body_text: Hillman to Acquire Kanebridge, Establishes Industrial Master Distribution Presence in U.S. Strategic Acquisition of Fastener Distributor Advances Hillman's Presence in Untapped Industrial Market Increases Industrial Total Addressable Market to $3 Billion while Diversifying Customer and End-Market Exposure Unique Digital and Operational Platform Primed for Future Growth Opportunities CINCINNATI, Aug. 03, 2026 -- Hillman Solutions Corp. ( Nasdaq:HLMN ) (the "Company", “Hillman Group”, or "Hillman"), a leading provider of hardware products and merchandising solutions, has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Kanebridge Corporation ("Kanebridge"), a leading master distributor of industrial fasteners for a purchase price of $315 million, subject to customary adjustments for cash, indebtedness, working capital and transaction expenses. Kanebridge supplies more than 44,000 commercial and military-grade fastener SKUs to distributors throughout the U.S. and Canada from its warehouses in Illinois and California, selling exclusively to distributors in commercial and industrial channels. Kanebridge prides itself on maintaining industry-leading fill rates, its proprietary digital ordering platform, FasNet ™, which enables same-day shipping, and its long-standing relationships with industrial and specialty distributors. These capabilities have made Kanebridge a critical partner for its customers for over 50 years. Consistent with Hillman's disciplined acquisition framework, the transaction is expected to be accretive to Hillman's margins and earnings. Hillman anticipates cost synergies from Hillman’s sourcing and distribution expertise , sales synergies coming from cross-selling opportunities, and material tax benefits from the transaction. Jon Michael Adinolfi, President and Chief Executive Officer of Hillman, commented, "Kanebridge gives us an immediate and credible foothold in the industrial channel, which we've identified as one of our biggest growth opportunities. Their master distributor model, capabilities-driven platform, and long-standing distributor relationships make it a great fit for us. This acquisition follows the same disciplined, accretive approach to M&A that has built Hillman over the past 60 years, and we're looking forward to welcoming the Kanebridge team to Hillman." Following completion of the acquisition, Kanebridge will operate as part of Hillman's commercial & industrial business, led by Chris Martin, EVP, Commercial & Industrial. Martin added: “Like Hillman, Kanebridge has decades of expertise taking great care of customers, maintaining strong fill rates, and providing a long tail of specialty fastener SKUs.Kanebridge's focus on the U.S. industrial market complements Hillman's existing industrial presence in Canada, broadening our combined reach across North America. The Kanebridge platform makes a great addition to our Commercial & Industrial business.” The acquisition advances Hillman's Industrial growth strategy, outlined at its recent Investor Day. The acquisition expands Hillman’s addressable market opportunity in industrial by $1 billion , bringing the total TAM to $3 billion . Kanebridge's master distributor model will leverage Hillman's global "dual faucet" sourcing expertise and extensive breadth of SKUs. Kanebridge gives Hillman an immediate, scaled platform to serve long-tail, high-specification fastener requirements across industrial and specialty distribution channels, while creating new cross-sell opportunities across Hillman's existing C&I, Pro and DIY customer base. The transaction has been approved by the boards of directors of both companies and is subject to regulatory approval and customary closing conditions. The Company expects to fund the transaction with a combination of cash from the balance sheet, borrowings under its existing asset-based revolving credit facility, and an add-on to its existing First Lien Term Loan, which the Company intends to raise through the capital markets. About Hillman Solutions Corp. Founded in 1964 and headquartered in Cincinnati, Hillman is a leading provider of hardware and related products serving retail, pro distribution, and industrial customers. Over the last 60-plus years, Hillman has built a legacy of service and growth by forming strategic partnerships with North America's leading home improvement, hardware, and farm and fleet retailers. Hillman differentiates itself from the competition with its dedicated field sales team of 1,200+ associates, direct-to-store distribution capabilities, and world class global sourcing and supply chain expertise. The company offers an extensive product portfolio of more than 111,000 SKUs, including fasteners (power screws, nuts, bolts), hardware (builder's hardware, door hardware, rope & chain, accessories), project gear & supplies (gloves, work gear, paint & cleaning sundries), and key and engraving services (key duplication, auto keys, and engraving). Hillman is committed to delivering exceptional customer service, innovative products, and dependable solutions to its customers and regularly earns vendor of the year recognition from top customers. For more information on Hillman, visit www.hillman.com . About Kanebridge Corporation Kanebridge Corporation is a leading U.S. master distributor of commercial and military-grade fasteners, serving distributors nationwide for more than 50 years. With more than 44,000 SKUs available for same-day shipment from warehouses in Illinois and California, Kanebridge is known for its product depth, fill-rate reliability, and specification expertise across inch and metric fastener categories. For more information, visit www.kanebridge.com . For more information: Contact: Michael Koehler Vice President – Corporate Development, Investor Relations, Treasury 513-826-5495 IR@hillmangroup.com Source: The Hillman Group

title: From Storage to Service: What It Really Takes to Return an Aircraft to the Skies After a Lease Ends
summary: When people talk about what keeps aircraft on the ground, the conversation usually goes straight to engines or avionics. Pneumatic components rarely come up — which is strange, because bleed air systems, environmental control systems, and anti-ice systems touch almost every major function on the aircraft, and when a single valve or air cycle machine fails, the effect on dispatch reliability is the same as any other AOG event.
body_text: When Spirit Airlines ceased operations in May 2026, dozens of Airbus A320-family aircraft went from active revenue service to idle almost overnight. Most of the fleet was leased rather than owned outright, which meant the jets didn't simply disappear into a bankruptcy estate, they went back to their lessors. Aircraft that had been flying passengers between Fort Lauderdale and the Caribbean one week were being ferried to storage facilities in Arizona and California the next, awaiting their next chapter. For the leasing companies now holding those aircraft, the immediate question isn't just "who's the next operator?" It's "what does it actually take to get this aircraft ready for them?" That question comes up more often than most people outside the industry realize. Leases end. Airlines restructure, downsize, or shut down entirely. Fleets get renewed. Whatever the reason, a lessor eventually ends up holding an aircraft that needs to go from parked to airworthy to earning revenue again, and the path between those two states is longer and more technical than it looks from the outside. Why "return to service" is its own discipline. An aircraft coming off lease isn't simply refueled and handed to the next airline. Every transition involves reconciling years of maintenance records, verifying the aircraft's configuration against what the next operator actually needs, and addressing whatever crept in during the handoff period itself. A few things make this especially demanding right now: Deferred maintenance backlogs. Airlines under financial pressure, and Spirit's well-documented restructuring is a clear example, often defer non-critical maintenance items as long as regulations allow. Those items don't disappear when the lease ends; they become the next operator's problem unless they're addressed during the transition. Storage effects. Aircraft don't like sitting still. Parked jets need active preservation programs to guard against corrosion, seal degradation, tire flat-spotting, and issues with fluids and batteries. The longer an aircraft sits, and the less rigorous the preservation program, the more work is needed to bring it back. Engine and APU status. In today's market, engines are often the single biggest variable in an aircraft's redelivery timeline. With narrowbody engine shop visits running well beyond historical turnaround times industry-wide, an aircraft with an engine approaching a shop visit can sit far longer than the airframe itself would otherwise require. Records reconciliation. Every log entry, repair, and modification has to be traceable and match physical inspection findings. Gaps or inconsistencies in records are one of the most common, and most time-consuming, obstacles to redelivery. What the redelivery process actually involves. A thorough return-to-service program typically includes: Technical records audit — reconciling maintenance history, airworthiness directives, and life-limited part status against physical records and inspection findings. Physical inspection — including borescope inspection of engines, structural inspections, and corrosion surveys, especially for aircraft that spent time in outdoor storage. Deferred item resolution — clearing any maintenance items that were deferred under Minimum Equipment List provisions during prior operation. Reconfiguration — adjusting cabin layout, livery, and avionics to match the next operator's specifications, which can range from a straightforward repaint to a full interior overhaul. Compliance updates — verifying the aircraft meets current regulatory requirements, from ADS-B Out to fuel tank flammability rules, particularly important if the aircraft is moving to a new regulatory jurisdiction. Airworthiness certification — final inspections and documentation (such as an 8130-3 or EASA Form 1, as applicable) confirming the aircraft is ready to fly under its next operator's certificate. None of these steps are optional, and skipping or rushing any of them tends to show up later as unscheduled maintenance, warranty disputes, or delayed entry into service — the opposite of what a lessor wants after finally placing an aircraft with a new operator. Why the partner matters as much as the process The technical steps above are fairly consistent across the industry. What varies enormously is how efficiently they get done, and that depends heavily on who's doing the work. A lessor managing a large volume of returning aircraft, as is happening across the industry in the wake of Spirit's fleet disposition, benefits from working with a partner that can handle storage, technical records review, heavy maintenance, and reconfiguration under one roof rather than coordinating separate vendors for each step. Every handoff between vendors is a potential delay, and every day an aircraft isn't earning lease revenue is a real cost. This is exactly the kind of work AerSale's Airframe MRO, Storage, and Transitions teams are built around: taking an aircraft from wherever it sits in the lifecycle — freshly returned from an operator, sitting in long-term storage, or mid-transition between lessees — and managing the technical work needed to get it back into service, efficiently and with full traceability. The bigger picture Spirit's situation is a visible example of a pattern that plays out constantly, if less publicly, across the leasing industry: leases end, operators change, and aircraft need new homes. With narrowbody demand strong and engine availability tight industry-wide, the lessors who can move aircraft through this process quickly and cleanly are the ones best positioned to capture that demand. If you're a lessor managing aircraft transitions — whether from a single lease expiration or a larger fleet event — AerSale's team can help assess what's needed and build a plan to get your aircraft airworthy and placed as efficiently as possible. Contact AerSale's Sales & Leasing or Airframe MRO team to discuss your fleet transition needs.

title: Meet the Winners of the Raj Shamani Builders’ Contest
summary: Meet the winners of the Raj Shamani Builders’ Contest and the real businesses they built with AI on Emergent.
body_text: The Raj Shamani Builders’ Contest has its winners. Deependra Singh Tomar took first place, Madhur Mishra took second, and Anshuman Dash and Thalachiri Ranjith Chowdary shared third. All four are Indian business owners who used Emergent to build working software for a real problem, with no coding background required. Run in partnership with entrepreneur and content creator Raj Shamani , the contest asked business owners to find a bottleneck in their own operations, build software to fix it, and put it into real use. More than 2,100 entries came in. Here are the four builds that stood out. Table: The four winning builds at a glance Winner Build What it does Who it serves Deependra Singh Tomar HisabX Daily accounts and cash reconciliation, with shift close in minutes Petrol pump dealers Madhur Mishra Agro Madat AI farming operating system with mandi prices and crop diagnosis Indian farmers Anshuman Dash Raizee.ai AI-native fundraising workspace for investor discovery and outreach Startup founders Thalachiri Ranjith Chowdary becAIm Business Turns company goals into daily AI missions per employee, with manager visibility Operators and teams Deependra Singh Tomar won first place with HisabX HisabX is a daily accounts and cash-reconciliation app for petrol pump dealers, and Deependra built it for his own forecourt before rolling it out to others. At a fuel station, every shift ends with a manual reconciliation of nozzle readings, cash, and credit sales, and that process is slow and easy to fudge. HisabX cut that from about 45 minutes on paper to roughly 8, with an audit trail that cannot be quietly rewritten, running offline-first on a low-cost Android phone. It is a clear example of what the contest rewarded: a dealer who knew the workflow better than any developer would, building the tool around it. Madhur Mishra took second place with Agro Madat Agro Madat is a farm-management operating system built for Indian farmers in the Neemuch and Mandsaur belt of Madhya Pradesh. It pulls the scattered tools a farmer needs into one app that works on a rural network. In one place, a farmer gets: Live wholesale mandi prices 7-day weather forecasts with hailstorm alerts Crop-disease diagnosis from a photo An irrigation advisor PMFBY crop-insurance claim help Medicinal-herb traceability for buyers It runs in English, Hindi, and Hinglish, with offline support. This is software a farmer would normally never have access to, built by someone who understands the belt firsthand. Anshuman Dash and Thalachiri Ranjith Chowdary shared third place Third place went to two builders who solved very different problems. The two split the ₹20 lakh third-place prize, ₹10 lakh each. 1. Anshuman Dash built Raizee.ai Raizee.ai is an AI-native fundraising workspace that runs the parts of a raise founders usually manage in spreadsheets. A founder describes what they are raising, and Raizee returns a ranked investor list with a fit score, drafts personalized outreach for each one, and tracks the pipeline from first contact to close. For a solo founder running a lean round, it replaces a stack of disconnected tools with one system. 2. Thalachiri Ranjith Chowdary built becAIm Business becAIm Business turns a company's goals into daily tasks for its team. Managers set a target, the app assigns each person their next step, and everyone can see who is on track and where things are slipping. It runs on manual goals from day one, with no integrations required to start. The contest drew builders from across India The four winners came out of a much larger field. Emergent and Raj Shamani also recognized a group of finalists whose builds stood out, drawn from business owners and operators across India. It is a snapshot of who is building with AI right now: not engineers by training, but people solving problems in businesses they run themselves. Build your own software on Emergent All four winners are non-developers who built for their own operations: a petrol dealer, a farmer serving other farmers, a founder raising capital, and a builder working on team execution. Each described a workflow they knew well, and Emergent built the software around it. The Raj Shamani Builders’ Contest was one of several builder contests Emergent runs. There is also Builder Fest, a global series of country-specific contests with local prize pools, live now in France and Indonesia through 25 August. You can find every contest, event, and builders’ challenge on the AI contests page. Every winner started with a problem they already understood, not a line of code. Describe yours in plain language and Emergent builds the software around it. Start Building with Emergent .

title: How to Invest in Stocks: A Beginner's Step-by-Step Guide
summary: Learn how to invest in stocks step by step. This beginner guide explains how to start investing, choose a brokerage account, buy stocks, diversify your portfolio, and manage risk.
body_text: Investing in stocks is one of the most effective ways to build long-term wealth, but getting started can feel overwhelming. If you're wondering how to invest in stocks , this guide explains every step—from opening your first brokerage account to building a diversified portfolio and managing investment risk. Part 1. What Does It Mean to Invest in Stocks? Stock investing means purchasing shares of publicly traded companies with the goal of benefiting from long-term price appreciation, dividends, or both. When you buy stock, you become a shareholder and own a small portion of the company. Your investment can increase or decrease in value depending on company performance, market conditions, and investor sentiment. Why Do People Invest in Stocks? People invest for several reasons: Build long-term wealth Save for retirement Generate dividend income Beat inflation Participate in economic growth Historically, the U.S. stock market has delivered positive long-term returns despite periods of volatility. However, past performance never guarantees future results. Investment Growth Potential Risk Liquidity Income Stocks High High High Dividends(some) Bonds Moderate Lower High Interest ETFs Moderate-Hight Moderate High Varies Mutual Funds Moderate Moderate Daily Varies CDs Low Very Low Limited Fixed Interest Part 2. How to Start Investing in Stocks Step by Step If you're wondering how to start investing in stocks , the process is easier than many beginners expect. You don't need to be a professional trader to buy stocks, but you do need a clear plan, the right account, and an understanding of your investment goals. At a high level, starting to invest in stocks involves six key steps: Define your financial goals and risk tolerance Open a brokerage account Deposit money into your account Research stocks before investing Place your first stock order Build and maintain a diversified portfolio Following these steps can help beginners create a more disciplined approach to investing. 2.1 Set Your Financial Goals Before investing in stocks, define your financial goals, investment timeline, and risk tolerance. Consider whether you are investing for retirement, long-term growth, or short-term goals. Make sure you have enough emergency savings before putting money into the market. Your investment strategy should match your financial situation, because different goals require different approaches to managing risk and choosing investments. 2.2 Choose a Brokerage Account To learn how to buy stocks, you need a brokerage account that provides access to publicly traded investments. Common account types include individual taxable accounts, joint accounts, Traditional IRAs, and Roth IRAs. When choosing a broker, consider fees, available investments, research tools, mobile app experience, educational resources, and customer support to find an account that fits your investing needs. 2.3 Fund Your Account After opening a brokerage account, deposit funds before purchasing stocks. Most brokerages support funding methods such as ACH bank transfers, wire transfers, debit transfers, or account transfers from another broker. Many online brokers offer no minimum deposit requirements, making it easier for beginners to start investing. However, only invest money that you do not need for daily expenses or emergency costs. 2.4 Research Stocks Before Buying Before purchasing a stock, research the company’s financial performance and future potential. Review factors such as revenue growth, earnings, profit margins, valuation ratios, industry outlook, and competitive advantages. Avoid buying stocks based only on social media trends or market headlines. A strong investment decision should be based on company fundamentals, research, and how the investment fits your overall financial goals. 2.5 Place Your First Stock Trade If you are searching for how to purchase stock , the process is simple. First, find the stock ticker symbol, choose the number of shares or investment amount, select an order type, review the details, and submit your trade. Common order types include market orders, limit orders, stop orders, and stop-limit orders, each offering different levels of price control and risk management. 2.6 Build a Diversified Portfolio Diversification is an important principle when learning how to invest in stocks . Instead of investing in a single company, consider spreading investments across sectors such as technology, healthcare, financials, consumer goods, and international markets. Many beginners also use ETFs alongside individual stocks because ETFs provide exposure to multiple companies in one investment, helping create a more balanced portfolio. 2.7 Regulation, Investor Protection, and Risks Choosing a brokerage account involves more than comparing commissions, trading tools, and investment features. Investors should also consider whether a brokerage is properly regulated, what protections are available for customer accounts, and what risks remain when investing in financial markets. A regulated brokerage must follow strict rules designed to protect investors, maintain fair markets, and safeguard customer assets. Before opening an account, investors should verify the brokerage’s regulatory status and understand the protections that apply to their investments. Part 3. How to Choose the Right Brokerage Platform Not all brokerage platforms offer the same experience. Consider costs, research tools, educational resources, and trading technology. Webull: Trading platform for All Investors Webull is an online brokerage platform designed for investors who want a balance between simplicity and advanced trading capabilities. It provides an easy entry point for beginners while offering professional-grade tools that can support investors as their experience grows. Unlike some platforms that focus only on basic investing, Webull combines commission-free trading with advanced charting, market data, technical analysis tools, and multiple trading platforms. This makes it suitable for investors who want to start with straightforward stock and ETF investing while gradually exploring more advanced strategies. This allows investors to build portfolios without paying traditional trading fees on eligible transactions. Fractional Shares Webull supports fractional share investing for eligible securities, allowing investors to purchase portions of stocks rather than needing to buy a full share. This feature can make higher-priced stocks more accessible for investors with smaller amounts of capital. This can be useful for investors who want to respond to market news or earnings announcements before or after regular trading sessions. This feature allows users to become familiar with trading tools, order types, and market movements before placing actual trades. Part 4. Common Beginner Investing Mistakes to Avoid Many new investors make avoidable mistakes when entering the stock market. Understanding these common pitfalls can help investors build healthier long-term investing habits. 1. Trying to Time the Market Some investors attempt to buy stocks at the lowest price and sell at the highest price. While this sounds appealing, consistently predicting short-term market movements is extremely difficult, even for experienced investors. Many long-term investors focus instead on building diversified portfolios and maintaining consistent investment strategies. 2. Investing Without Diversification Putting too much money into a single stock, industry, or market segment can increase risk. For example, an investor who invests only in one company may experience significant losses if that company faces financial difficulties. Diversification across different companies, sectors, and asset classes can help reduce the impact of individual investment losses. 3. Ignoring Fees and Costs Even when a brokerage offers commission-free trading, investors should understand that other costs may apply depending on the products and services they use. Potential costs may include: Options-related fees Margin interest Account transfer fees Regulatory fees Fund expense ratios Small costs can affect long-term investment results, especially over many years. 4. Chasing Trending Stocks New investors may feel pressure to buy stocks that are receiving significant attention online or in the news. However, popular stocks can experience rapid price changes, and buying based only on hype or short-term trends can lead to unexpected losses. Investors should evaluate factors such as: Company financial performance Business model Competitive position Valuation Long-term growth potential 5. Making Emotional Investment Decisions Fear and excitement can strongly influence investment decisions. Common emotional mistakes include: Selling during market downturns because of panic Buying after a stock has already risen sharply due to fear of missing out (FOMO) Changing strategies based on short-term market movements Developing a clear investment plan can help investors make more disciplined decisions. 6. Investing Money Needed in the Short Term The stock market can be unpredictable over short periods. Investors should generally avoid investing money they may need soon for essential expenses, such as: Emergency savings Rent or mortgage payments Near-term purchases Short-term financial obligations Maintaining an appropriate cash reserve can help investors avoid selling investments at unfavorable times. 7. Failing to Research Investments Before buying a stock, investors should understand what they are purchasing. Basic research may include reviewing: Company revenue and earnings Business strategy Industry conditions Competitive advantages Financial health Management performance Taking time to research investments can help investors make more informed decisions rather than relying on speculation. Part 5. FAQs 1. How do I invest in stocks if I'm a complete beginner? Start by opening a brokerage account, funding it, researching companies or ETFs, and investing gradually with a long-term plan. 2. How much money do I need to start investing in stocks? Many brokerages allow investors to start with little money through fractional shares, though the amount you should invest depends on your financial goals and budget. 3. How can you invest in stocks without taking too much risk? Diversify across companies and sectors, invest consistently, focus on long-term goals, and avoid concentrating your portfolio in a single stock. 4. Is it better to invest in individual stocks or ETFs? Many beginners choose ETFs for broad diversification, while experienced investors may combine ETFs with individual stocks. 5. What is the safest way to buy stocks online? Use a regulated U.S. brokerage that is registered with the SEC, is a FINRA member, offers SIPC protection for eligible assets, and provides strong account security features such as multi-factor authentication. 6. When is the best time to start investing? Many financial professionals recommend investing as early as possible so your investments have more time to potentially benefit from compound growth. The right timing also depends on your financial situation and risk tolerance. Part 6. The Bottom Line Learning how to invest in stocks starts with understanding your goals, choosing a trusted brokerage, and following a disciplined long-term strategy. A platform with strong education, research tools, and investor protections can help you begin with confidence while supporting your growth as your investing experience expands. title: Netflix Marks 10 Years in India, Deepens Partnership with Ministry of Tourism and Culture
summary: Ted Sarandos and Union Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat launch the "As Seen on Netflix" section on the Incredible India website.
body_text: Entertainment 06 August 2026 Global India Link copied to clipboard As Netflix marks ten years in India, the Ministry of Culture and the Ministry of Tourism and Netflix India came together for a special evening celebrating how storytelling brings India’s rich cultural heritage, diverse destinations and lived experiences to audiences around the world. As part of our ongoing partnership, the Ministry of Tourism and Netflix today launched "As Seen on Netflix" , a first-of-its-kind section on the Incredible India website aimed at helping audiences discover the real locations, cultural traditions and authentic experiences featured in Netflix India's films and series. Netflix Co-CEO Ted Sarandos joined Hon’ble Minister for Culture and Tourism Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat for a fireside conversation at the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA) on how authentic storytelling can inspire audiences to discover the cultures and places featured in these stories, while supporting India’s creative economy. Both reaffirmed their commitment to enabling more stories rooted in India’s diverse cultures, landscapes and traditions to reach audiences worldwide. The event also marked the premiere of two new videos celebrating India's wildlife and cultural heritage, expanding the partnership's efforts to showcase India’s multicultural facets. Following an MoU signed by the Ministry of Tourism and Netflix India last year, the Hon'ble Minister launched two videos at ITB Berlin, which Indian Missions have since used to promote India's tourism and cultural diplomacy. The collaboration reflects the Government of India's commitment to creating an enabling environment for storytelling by supporting productions across the country and showcasing India's cultural richness through entertainment. Hon'ble Minister of Culture and Tourism Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat said, "India's stories have always been our greatest cultural ambassadors. As technology brings the world closer together, our collaboration with Netflix creates an extraordinary opportunity to take India to the world and bring the world to India. Through powerful storytelling, we can showcase the richness of India's culture, heritage, destinations and wildlife, inspiring global audiences to experience Incredible India firsthand. Together, we are strengthening India's creative ecosystem while reinforcing our position as a leading cultural and tourism destination." Netflix Co-CEO Ted Sarandos said, “ There isn’t one India, there are many Indias. Over the past ten years, we’ve seen how stories rooted in different parts of the country can connect with audiences around the world. When people discover a place or culture through a story, it can inspire them to experience it for themselves. We’re pleased to continue working with the Ministry of Culture and Tourism to help more of India’s stories and destinations reach global audiences.” Over the past decade, Netflix has brought stories from across India to international audiences while working with local creators, production partners and communities across the country. From the bond between humans and wildlife in The Elephant Whisperers and the music of Amar Singh Chamkila , to the visual opulence of Heeramandi: The Diamond Bazaar , the evocative mountains of Musafir Café and the cross-cultural immersion of Made in Korea, Netflix’s films and series illustrate how India’s many cultures, traditions and destinations become an integral part of the stories themselves. Ritika Jain Communications Manager ritikaj@netflix.com

title: Alector Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Provides Business Update

Continued progress across AL064/AL164 ( ABC -enabled Tau siRNA for
body_text: Advancing the Alector Brain Carrier (ABC) blood-brain barrier platform across antibodies, enzymes, and siRNA, with AL137 advancing as Alector’s lead ABC-enabled anti-amyloid beta (Aβ) antibody program for Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Continued progress across AL064/AL164 (ABC-enabled Tau siRNA for AD and other tauopathies) and AL050 (ABC-enabled GCase Enzyme Replacement Therapy for Parkinson’s disease (PD)). $172.8 million in cash, cash equivalents and investments provide runway at least through 2027 SOUTH SAN FRANCISCO, Calif., Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Alector, Inc. (Nasdaq: ALEC), a biotechnology company focused on developing therapies to counteract the devastating progression of neurodegeneration, today reported second quarter 2026 financial results and recent portfolio and business updates. As of June 30, 2026, Alector’s cash, cash equivalents, and investments totaled $172.8 million. " We continue to make steady progress across our ABC-enabled preclinical and research pipeline,” said Arnon Rosenthal, Ph.D., Chief Executive Officer of Alector. “Our work across antibodies, enzymes, and siRNA reflects the versatility of the ABC platform and our strategy to apply it to programs where enhanced brain delivery may address important limitations in the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases. We remain focused on disciplined execution as we advance our portfolio toward clinical development, with the goal of addressing important unmet needs for patients living with neurodegenerative diseases.” Recent Program Updates Alector Brain Carrier (ABC): Preclinical and Research Pipeline Alector’s proprietary Alector Brain Carrier (ABC) blood-brain barrier platform is central to the company’s strategy to enhance therapeutic delivery to the brain. ABC is designed to achieve efficient, enhanced brain delivery through differentiated binding to a distinct region of the transferrin receptor (TfR) and to enable peripheral dosing, while preserving a favorable safety profile. It is adaptable across multiple drug modalities, including antibodies, enzymes, and siRNA. Core to the platform's design are the principles of versatility, translatability, and differentiated binding. Preclinical studies across multiple ABC-enabled programs have shown robust brain penetration, supporting the advancement of a broad pipeline directed at the underlying drivers of neurodegenerative diseases. AL137 Following successful completion of IND-enabling studies evaluating both subcutaneous (SC) and intravenous (IV) administration, Alector selected AL137 as the lead molecule for its anti-amyloid beta (Aβ) antibody program for AD, with AL037 retained as a backup candidate. The company is targeting an IND submission in Q1 2027 and first-in-human dosing in Australia no later than April 2027. AL137 combines Alector’s proprietary high-affinity fully human anti-Aβ antibody which selectively binds pyroglutamate-3 (PyroGlu3-Aβ), a validated and pathogenic form of Aβ enriched in amyloid plaques, with the company’s proprietary ABC platform. Based on preclinical studies, AL137 is designed to be delivered SC and to combine several differentiated attributes intended to optimize efficacy, safety, convenience, and manufacturability, including: High brain exposure and efficient brain delivery through the ABC platform, supporting low projected efficacious dose. Preserved full IgG1 Fc effector function, designed to maximize recruitment of brain immune cells for efficient amyloid plaque clearance. A proprietary transferrin receptor (TfR)-binding epitope designed to maintain brain delivery while reducing hematologic adverse effects associated with targeting TfR with a full Fc effector function. A favorable preclinical safety profile to support the planned clinical study, with no observed adverse effects and only transient, reversible, non-adverse hematological findings with SC dosing. Supportive pharmacokinetic and formulation characteristics intended to enable convenient monthly subcutaneous administration using a high-concentration formulation. High-productivity manufacturability, with an identified stable, high-expressing cell line designed to support efficient large-scale manufacturing and commercial scalability. ABC-Enabled siRNA Platform Alector continues to advance its ABC-enabled siRNA platform, designed for peripheral dosing and offering the potential for more convenient administration compared with traditional intrathecal delivery, as well as the potential for homogeneous drug distribution throughout the brain. AL064/AL164 Alector’s lead siRNA program, AL064/AL164, is a tau siRNA program for AD and other tauopathies and aims to reduce toxic tau protein expression and slowing of cognitive decline in AD. AL064 demonstrated robust tau mRNA knockdown and durable reduction of phospho-Tau 217 in non-human primate brains. AL064 was modified to incorporate a well-validated chemical modification intended to further optimize siRNA stability, and this modified form is advancing into IND-enabling studies as AL164. Early-Stage siRNA Programs Earlier-stage siRNA programs advancing toward lead candidate selection include ADP062-ABC, an alpha-synuclein siRNA for PD, and ADP065-ABC, an NLRP3 siRNA for multiple neurodegenerative conditions, reflecting the broad applicability of the ABC platform across disease mechanisms. Alector continues to evaluate development plans and timing for its ABC-enabled siRNA programs. AL050 AL050, Alector’s ABC-enabled engineered glucocerebrosidase (GCase) enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), is in preclinical development for PD. AL050 is engineered to overcome the central challenges of delivering enzyme therapy to the brain, combining an engineered GCase with enhanced activity and stability, a silenced effector function for safety, and Alector's tunable ABC technology. To date, preclinical data have demonstrated increased GCase activity in both rodents and NHPs and reduced toxic substrate accumulation in a rodent GBA disease model with no apparent hematologic findings, supporting continued development as a potential therapy for PD and Lewy body dementia (LBD) associated with GBA loss-of-function mutations and subsequently for idiopathic PD and LBD. Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results Revenue. Collaboration revenue for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, was $3.3 million, compared to $7.9 million for the same period in 2025. The decrease was primarily due to lower revenue recognized for the AL101 AD program. R&D Expenses. Total research and development expenses for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, were $19.5 million, compared to $27.6 million for the quarter ended June 30, 2025. The decrease was mainly due to a decrease in personnel-related costs as a result of the reductions in force as well as a decrease in facilities and other expenses. G&A Expenses. Total general and administrative expenses for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, were $8.3 million, compared to $14.4 million for the quarter ended June 30, 2025. The decrease was mainly driven by a decrease in personnel-related costs as a result of the reductions in force. Net Loss. For the quarter ended June 30, 2026, Alector reported a net loss of $23.0 million, or $0.21 net loss per share, compared to a net loss of $30.5 million, or $0.30 net loss per share, for the same period in 2025. Cash Position. Cash, cash equivalents, and investments were $172.8 million as of June 30, 2026. Management anticipates that this will be sufficient to fund Alector’s operations at least through 2027. About Alector Alector is a biotechnology company focused on developing therapies to counteract the devastating progression of neurodegenerative diseases. Leveraging the principles of genetics, immunology, and neuroscience, the company is advancing a portfolio of programs that aim to remove toxic proteins, replace missing proteins, and restore immune and nerve cell function. Supported by biomarkers, Alector’s product candidates seek to treat a range of indications, such as Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson's disease. The company is also developing Alector Brain Carrier (ABC), a proprietary blood-brain barrier platform, which is being applied to its preclinical and research pipeline. ABC aims to enhance the delivery of therapeutics, achieve deeper brain penetration and efficacy at lower doses, and ultimately improve patient outcomes while reducing costs. Alector is headquartered in South San Francisco, California. For more information, please visit www.alector.com .
